Glossary
LevelWhat it meansExample, from this register
CapabilityWhat the business is able to do, named apart from how it is built. Covered by the flows that deliver it.Fulfil customer orders
Intended flowOne case's path from start to end, as designed.Fulfilling a customer's order
StageOne ordered stretch of a flow, with an entry and an exit.Place the order
Process stepOne act inside a stage, with an outcome the business would recognise, that happened or did not.The customer's basket is emptied
PartA person or a component that carries out or supports a step. The field's term is participant.Fulfilment staff; WebApp
ComponentA deployable part of the system that performs or supports a step. An AI agent is one.WebApp
External dependencySomething the system relies on and does not run.Webhook subscriber endpoint
Expected outcomeA way a stage ends on its main path: the case leaves the stage as designed. Not numbered.The order is placed
Other outcomeAny other way a stage ends: an alternative or exception path out of it. Not numbered.The order is cancelled because an item is out of stock
RunOne request an AI agent takes for one case, from taking it to its reply. The field's term is agent invocation.
OperationOne act inside a run: a call to its model, a tool, or a check. Not a process step.
Agent partA piece of the agent's own machinery: its model, the functions it may call, its guardrails or its orchestration.
CaseOne instance going through a flow, from its start to its end: what the business measures count.One order: a row of ordering.orders

Trigger
WebApp deletes the basket through Basket API by gRPC after the order call; ClientApp clears its basket the same way
Interactions, in order
  1. WebApp deletes the basket through Basket API by gRPC after the order call; ClientApp clears its basket the same way
  2. OrderStartedIntegrationEvent written with the order
  3. OrderStartedIntegrationEvent via RabbitMQ exchange eshop_event_bus to queue Basket, which deletes the basket
  4. In an order not in the map yet:
    • WebApp → Basket API: deletes the basket on request and on OrderStartedIntegrationEvent
    • Basket API → Basket store: the basket key that is deleted
    • ClientApp → Basket API: deletes the basket on request and on OrderStartedIntegrationEvent
    • Ordering API → Event bus: carries OrderStartedIntegrationEvent to queue Basket
    • Event bus → Basket API: deletes the basket on request and on OrderStartedIntegrationEvent
Right outcome
the buyer's basket is gone once the order exists (proposed)
If it does not happen
The basket keeps the ordered items and the customer may order them twice. Two paths empty it: the WebApp after its call and Basket API on OrderStartedIntegrationEvent
Timeouts
not in the map yet

› › Expected outcome: The order is placed

Key to the drawing
  • Each part has a box at the top and a dashed line down from it; time runs down the page.
  • Round box: a person. An AI agent is drawn inside the box of the part it runs inside. Long-dashed box: an external dependency, run by someone else.

  • Mono label: the operation that performs the step. Italic label: the register's own description.
  • ~: a call made within that hop whose place in it is not in the map yet. Coregion bracket: calls whose order is not in the map yet.
  • Dotted arrow with ?: how the turn passes between the two parts is not in the map yet. Dot at the left edge: a call whose sender is not in the map yet.
  • loop: a call made more than once. alt: one of several ways, each in its own band.
Trigger
WebApp reads the basket from Basket API by gRPC and the items' names and prices from Catalog API
Interactions, in order
  1. WebApp reads the basket from Basket API by gRPC and the items' names and prices from Catalog API
  2. WebApp → Ordering API: POST /api/orders with x-requestid, or ClientApp through Mobile BFF
  3. Ordering API: Ordering API writes the order in Submitted with its buyer and payment method, and the OrderStarted and OrderStatusChangedToSubmitted outbox rows, in one transaction
  4. In an order not in the map yet:
    • WebApp → Basket API: returns the basket lines that become the order's items
    • WebApp → Catalog API: returns each item's name and current price
    • ClientApp → Mobile BFF: routes /api/orders to Ordering API
    • Mobile BFF → Ordering API: writes the order in Submitted with buyer, payment method and outbox rows
    • Ordering API → Ordering database: stores the order, buyer, payment method and outbox rows
    • Basket API → Basket store: holds the basket the order is built from
    • Catalog API → Catalog database: holds the items' names and prices
    • Ordering API → Identity API: issues and signs the customer's token that Ordering API checks
Right outcome
an ordering.orders row in Submitted with one orderItems row per basket line at the catalogue price, the delivery address, and BuyerId and PaymentMethodId set (proposed)
If it does not happen
No order record. Ordering API answers 200 even when the command returned false, and an exception inside the command is swallowed into false; the WebApp does not read the response, empties the basket anyway and shows the orders page. The customer must notice and order again. Recovery: not created
Timeouts
WebApp's HTTP clients carry the standard resilience handler; a repeated POST with the same x-requestid is answered without a second order

› › Step 2.1: The order is released for stock checking when the grace period ends

Key to the drawing
  • Each part has a box at the top and a dashed line down from it; time runs down the page.
  • Round box: a person. An AI agent is drawn inside the box of the part it runs inside. Long-dashed box: an external dependency, run by someone else.

  • Mono label: the operation that performs the step. Italic label: the register's own description.
  • ~: a call made within that hop whose place in it is not in the map yet. Coregion bracket: calls whose order is not in the map yet.
  • Dotted arrow with ?: how the turn passes between the two parts is not in the map yet. Dot at the left edge: a call whose sender is not in the map yet.
  • loop: a call made more than once. alt: one of several ways, each in its own band.
Trigger
Order Processor selects orders in Submitted older than the grace period, on every run. The case is in Submitted
Interactions, in order
  1. Order Processor receives: Order Processor selects orders in Submitted older than the grace period, on every run. Its sender is not in the map yet
  2. GracePeriodConfirmedIntegrationEvent via RabbitMQ exchange eshop_event_bus to queue Ordering
  3. How the turn passes from Order Processor to Ordering API: not in the map yet.
  4. Ordering API: Ordering API sets AwaitingValidation and writes OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidationIntegrationEvent to its outbox in the same transaction
  5. In an order not in the map yet:
    • Ordering API → Ordering database: answers the poll and stores the new status
    • Order Processor → Ordering database: answers the poll and stores the new status
    • Order Processor → Event bus: carries GracePeriodConfirmedIntegrationEvent to queue Ordering
    • Event bus → Ordering API: sets AwaitingValidation and writes its outbox row
Right outcome
AwaitingValidation within 1.5 minutes of "OrderDate", with its OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidation outbox row at State 2 (Published) (proposed)
If it does not happen
The order stays in Submitted, and each poll publishes for it again, so it moves on once the poller, the broker and Ordering API's consumer work. A failed query is logged and returns no orders; a failed publish is not caught in the loop and stops the background service. Recovery: moves on
Timeouts
Grace period GracePeriodTime 1 minute, polled every CheckUpdateTime 30 seconds. Every run re-publishes for each order still Submitted. The bus's retry policy (RetryCount 10) never retries a failed publish: Execute is given an async lambda, so the failure lands in the returned task, not the call (Polly's Execute overloads)

Trigger
Ordering API publishes OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidationIntegrationEvent from ordering."IntegrationEventLog" right after the commit. The case is in AwaitingValidation
Interactions, in order
  1. Ordering API receives: Ordering API publishes OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidationIntegrationEvent from ordering."IntegrationEventLog" right after the commit. It is sent from ordering."IntegrationEventLog" right after the commit; that sender is not in the map yet
  2. Via RabbitMQ exchange eshop_event_bus to queue Catalog
  3. How the turn passes from Ordering API to Catalog API: not in the map yet.
  4. Catalog API: Catalog API compares each item's AvailableStock with its units
  5. Catalog API receives: . It is sent from Catalog API writes OrderStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent; that sender is not in the map yet
  6. Via RabbitMQ to queue Ordering
  7. How the turn passes from Catalog API to Ordering API: not in the map yet.
  8. Ordering API: Ordering API waits 10 seconds then sets StockConfirmed and writes OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent to its outbox
  9. In an order not in the map yet:
    • Ordering API → Ordering database: holds the order's status and the outbox rows
    • Catalog API → Catalog database: holds AvailableStock read by the check; a stale figure makes the check wrong
    • Ordering API → Event bus: carries the request to queue Catalog and the answer to queue Ordering
    • Event bus → Ordering API: publishes the stock-check request from its outbox; sets StockConfirmed after 10 seconds and writes its outbox row
    • Event bus → Catalog API: checks AvailableStock for each item and answers through its outbox
    • Catalog API → Event bus: carries the request to queue Catalog and the answer to queue Ordering
Right outcome
StockConfirmed only when every ordered product is in the catalogue with AvailableStock of at least its units; Description 'All the items were confirmed with available stock.' (proposed)
If it does not happen
The order stays in AwaitingValidation with nothing to move it: a failed publish is marked PublishedFailed and never sent again; a consumer that throws still acknowledges the message, so it is gone; the poll re-sends only for Submitted. A message waiting in its queue for a stopped consumer moves on when the consumer returns. Recovery: stranded
Timeouts
10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set. Ordering API consumes its queue with one consumer on one channel, so these waits queue behind one another

A message waiting in its queue for a stopped consumer moves on when the consumer returns. Recovery: stranded

  • Money the customer pays; value blocked while the order is stuck
  • What must be in stock and shipped
  • Who is waiting and who is told
  • Where the goods must arrive
  • What is charged

How a case moves end to end

Click a flow on the map to see its stages in order, each with its promise.

Fulfilling a customer's order

Key to the drawing
  • Box: a stage, in order, with its promise. Filled dot: where a case starts.
  • Arrow between stages: a case moves from one to the other. Solid: an expected outcome makes the move. Dashed: only an other outcome does.
  • Arc over a stage: a case can go straight past it, to the stage the arc ends at.
  • Dashed arrow down: an other outcome that ends the case in that stage.
  • Rounded box with a ringed dot: where the expected path ends.

Where this comes from
  • case: One order: a row of ordering.orders (Ordering.Infrastructure/EntityConfigurations/OrderEntityTypeConfiguration.cs:7; Ordering.Infrastructure/Migrations/OrderingContextModelSnapshot.cs:155-189)
  • starts_at: The order's record is written in Submitted: Ordering.API/Application/Commands/CreateOrderCommandHandler.cs:40-51 (new Order, Add, SaveEntitiesAsync), status set at Ordering.Domain/AggregatesModel/OrderAggregate/Order.cs:57, committed by Ordering.API/Application/Behaviors/TransactionBehavior.cs:47
  • ends_at: The customer has the goods: the order is delivered. The code's last recorded state is Shipped (Ordering.Domain/AggregatesModel/OrderAggregate/Order.cs:130-140; Ordering.Domain/AggregatesModel/OrderAggregate/OrderStatus.cs:12); the stretch to delivery is added from the reference model (ST4). Or definitively not: the order is Cancelled, for lack of stock (Ordering.Domain/AggregatesModel/OrderAggregate/Order.cs:155-168), a failed payment or the customer's request (Ordering.Domain/AggregatesModel/OrderAggregate/Order.cs:142-153)
  • expectation_of: The customer who placed the order (the buyer, ordering.buyers; Ordering.API/Application/Queries/OrderQueries.cs:37-49 lists a buyer's orders)
  • promise: none stated; proposed: none assumed by the code end to end. The code assumes about 2 minutes from placing to Paid (ST2) and nothing for shipping or delivery
  • delivers: C2; C3; C10
  • source: Ordering.API/Application/Commands/CreateOrderCommandHandler.cs:40-51; Ordering.Domain/AggregatesModel/OrderAggregate/Order.cs:5-186
  • ST1 promise: proposed: none assumed by the code beyond one request: placing is a single call (L01), bounded only by the HTTP client's resilience defaults (eShop.ServiceDefaults/Extensions.cs:22-29)
  • ST2 promise: proposed: 2 minutes from entering Submitted, read from the timing of L03, L04 and L06: a 1-minute grace period and up to 30 seconds to the next poll (OrderProcessor/appsettings.json:15-16; OrderProcessor/Services/GracePeriodManagerService.cs:17, 51), then 10 seconds before StockConfirmed and 10 before Paid (Ordering.API/Application/Commands/SetStockConfirmedOrderStatusCommandHandler.cs:22; Ordering.API/Application/Commands/SetPaidOrderStatusCommandHandler.cs:22). The stage is entered when the record is created, so a case's age in it is now minus "OrderDate" (Ordering.Domain/AggregatesModel/OrderAggregate/Order.cs:58)
  • ST3 promise: proposed: none assumed by the code: nothing schedules or times shipping (Ordering.API/Apis/OrdersApi.cs:12). The operators' dispatch target would set one
  • ST4 promise: proposed: none assumed by the code; the carrier's delivery commitment would set one
